P200-F01-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Six requests, A–F, are checked using the records below. Their acceptance depends on filling in missing yes/no marks.

Marks: Y = yes; U = ?; V = ?; W = ?.
A question mark means unrecorded, not no. Exactly two of U, V and W must be yes. These are the only restrictions on the missing marks. Each missing mark is filled once, and every reference to that mark uses the same value.

Each ticket can have several versions. Keep only its largest-numbered version, even when that version points to a different link. Discard older versions before looking up requests or marks. Each retained row names a link identifying both a request and a mark. An allow row whose mark is yes supplies support to its request. A block row whose mark is yes supplies an exclusion. A row whose mark is no supplies neither. A request is accepted exactly when it has at least one support and no exclusion. There are no unlisted tickets.

Links (link | request | mark):
a | A | Y
b | B | U
c | C | V
d | D | W
e | E | U
f | E | V
g | F | Y
h | B | V
i | C | U
j | F | W

Ticket rows (ticket | version | kind | link):
t1 | 1 | allow | a
t2 | 1 | allow | b
t3 | 1 | block | h
t4 | 1 | allow | c
t5 | 1 | block | i
t6 | 1 | allow | d
t7 | 1 | block | d
t8 | 1 | allow | e
t9 | 1 | allow | f
t10 | 1 | allow | g
t11 | 1 | block | a
t11 | 2 | block | j

Which option gives both (i) exactly the requests accepted under every allowed filling and (ii) the largest number of requests accepted simultaneously under a single allowed filling?

1. Always accepted: {A, E}. Largest simultaneous count: 3.
2. Always accepted: {A}. Largest simultaneous count: 3.
3. Always accepted: {A, E}. Largest simultaneous count: 4.

P200-F01-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A tool-lending club keeps two linked tables, which list all of its members and all of its tools. A dash (—) marks a value that exists but was not recorded: it may be any allowed value and is never a default. Allowed values: Dues is Paid or Unpaid; Check is Pass or Fail; every tool has exactly one Owner, who is one of the five members.

Members (Dues; Sponsor): Ada (Paid; none), Bo (—; Ada), Cy (—; Ada), Dee (Paid; Ada), Eli (Paid; Dee).

Tools (Owner; Check): T1 (Ada; Pass), T2 (Ada; Pass), T3 (Bo; Pass), T4 (Bo; —), T5 (Cy; Pass), T6 (Dee; Pass), T7 (Dee; —), T8 (Eli; Pass), T9 (—; —).

Rules:
- A member is on notice exactly when they own at least one tool whose Check is Fail.
- A member is in good standing exactly when their Dues are Paid, they are not on notice, and either they have no sponsor or their sponsor is in good standing.
- A tool is lendable exactly when its Check is Pass, its owner is in good standing, and no member whose Sponsor is that owner is on notice.

Facts (all true):
1. Exactly one member has Unpaid dues.
2. Exactly one tool has a Fail check.
3. No member owns more than two tools.
4. The member with Unpaid dues does not own the tool with the Fail check.

Consider every way of filling in all the dashes that respects the allowed values and all four facts. Across all such completions, what are the smallest and the largest possible numbers of lendable tools?

1. Smallest 0, largest 4
2. Smallest 1, largest 5
3. Smallest 3, largest 6
4. Smallest 1, largest 4
5. Smallest 0, largest 9

A panel has fourteen lights: A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J, K, L, M, N and P. Each light is either on or off. Two facts are known: A is on, and K is off. The panel also obeys these thirteen rules:
1. If G and C are both on, then D is on.
2. If A is on, then E is on.
3. If H and F are both on, then K is on.
4. If M is on, then E is on.
5. If A and C are both on, then H is on.
6. If N is on, then P is on.
7. If B and J are both on, then K is on.
8. If E is on, then C is on.
9. If J, D and H are all on, then K is on.
10. If C and N are both on, then F is on.
11. If P is on, then L is on.
12. If M and L are both on, then K is on.
13. If G is on, then J is on.
Each rule says only this: whenever all the lights named before 'then' are on, the light named after 'then' is on. It does not say the reverse. There are no other constraints, so a light may be on even if no rule requires it. A state is an on/off setting of all fourteen lights that satisfies both facts and all thirteen rules. At least one state exists. A light is certainly off if it is off in every state.
Exactly which lights other than K are certainly off?

1. F, G, L, N and P
2. F and N
3. F, G and N
4. B, D, F, G, J, L, M, N and P
5. D, F, G, J, L, N and P

P200-F02-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

An automated safety monitor at a processing plant tracks 12 status indicators—A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H, J, K, L, and M—each of which is either active or inactive in the plant's true state. The system is governed by 11 strictly forward conditional rules:

- R1: If D, G, and M are active, then B is active.
- R2: If C, H, and J are active, then K is active.
- R3: If A and C are active, then G is active.
- R4: If B, F, and K are active, then L is active.
- R5: If A, G, and J are active, then M is active.
- R6: If B, E, and M are active, then H is active.
- R7: If A and D are active, then C is active.
- R8: If D, E, and K are active, then L is active.
- R9: If C and D are active, then J is active.
- R10: If A, H, and L are active, then E is active.
- R11: If F, G, and J are active, then H is active.

Each rule states a sufficient condition only (no converses hold: an indicator may be active even when no rule concluding it has all of its premises active), and no closed-world assumption applies (an indicator that is not forced to be active by confirmed facts and the rules is not assumed to be inactive; any combination of active and inactive indicators is possible provided it satisfies the confirmed facts and R1–R11).

Initially, only indicators A and D are confirmed to be active. Which statement accurately characterizes the indicators guaranteed to be active from the initial confirmation alone, as well as the total number of indicators guaranteed to be active if one additional indicator is also confirmed to be active?

1. From the initial confirmation alone, exactly 7 indicators (A, B, C, D, G, J, M) are guaranteed to be active while the other 5 remain undetermined; additionally confirming H guarantees 9 active indicators, additionally confirming E guarantees 11, and F is the only single additional indicator whose confirmation guarantees all 12.
2. From the initial confirmation alone, exactly 7 indicators (A, B, C, D, G, J, M) are guaranteed to be active while the other 5 remain undetermined; additionally confirming either E or H guarantees 11 active indicators (all except F), and F is the only single additional indicator whose confirmation guarantees all 12.
3. From the initial confirmation alone, exactly 7 indicators (A, B, C, D, G, J, M) are guaranteed to be active while the other 5 remain undetermined; additionally confirming H guarantees 9 active indicators, and additionally confirming either E or F guarantees that all 12 indicators are active.
4. From the initial confirmation alone, exactly 6 indicators (A, C, D, G, J, M) are guaranteed to be active while the other 6 remain undetermined; additionally confirming B guarantees 7 active indicators, additionally confirming E guarantees 11, and additionally confirming F guarantees all 12.
5. From the initial confirmation alone, the 7 indicators A, B, C, D, G, J, M are guaranteed to be active and the remaining 5 indicators (E, F, H, K, L) are guaranteed to be inactive unless an external override alters the rules.

P200-F03-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Eight flags A, B, C, D, E, F, P and Q each have a definite state: on or off. A letter standing alone means that flag is on; “not A” means A is off.

Use ordinary two-valued logic. For any statements X and Y, “X only if Y” means that if X is true, Y must be true. “X unless Y” means that if Y is false, X must be true. Neither expression states a converse. “Or” is inclusive, and “and” requires both statements. An implication is false exactly when its antecedent is true and its consequent is false.

All eight of these fixed rules must be true:
• A only if not D.
• E unless B.
• C only if not F.
• Not D only if A or P.
• E only if not B or P.
• Not F only if C or P.
• Q only if A and C.
• Not B unless not Q.

Separately, exactly one of the following six recorded notices is false; the other five are true. Evaluate their truth using the same definitions above. A false notice is not merely an omitted rule: its antecedent must be true and its consequent false.
• A only if not B.
• C unless B.
• C only if not D.
• E unless D.
• E only if not F.
• A unless F.

A valid assignment gives states to all eight flags, satisfies every fixed rule, and makes exactly one recorded notice false. “Always on” or “always off” means that state occurs in every valid assignment. “Varies” means the flag is on in at least one valid assignment and off in at least one other; it does not mean the flag can ignore the rules.

Which option correctly classifies P, Q and A across all valid assignments?

1. P: always on; Q: varies; A: always off.
2. P: varies; Q: always off; A: always on.
3. P: always on; Q: always off; A: varies.
4. P: always off; Q: varies; A: varies.
5. P: varies; Q: always on; A: always off.

P200-F03-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A control board manages seven relays—A, B, C, D, E, F, and G—each of which is set to either Active or Idle. Relays A, B, C, and D form the Primary Bank, while relays E, F, and G form the Secondary Bank.

Throughout the specifications below, for any statements P and Q:
- "P if Q" means that whenever Q is true, P must be true.
- "P only if Q" means that whenever P is true, Q must be true.
- "P unless Q" means that whenever Q is false, P must be true.

A configuration of the seven relays is valid if and only if it satisfies all seven of the following conditions:
1. Bank Balance: The number of Active relays in the Primary Bank equals the number of Active relays in the Secondary Bank.
2. A is Active unless both B is Active and E is Idle.
3. B is Active only if F is Active, and C is Active only if G is Active.
4. E is Active unless D is Idle.
5. F is Active only if either C is Active or D is Active (or both).
6. B is Active unless C is Active.
7. E is Active only if C is Idle.

A relay's state is forced if it has the same state in every valid configuration (either forced Active if it is Active in every valid configuration, or forced Idle if it is Idle in every valid configuration). A relay's state is unknown if it is Active in at least one valid configuration and Idle in at least one valid configuration.

Which of the following correctly classifies all seven relays?

1. Relays C, F, and G are forced Active; relays D and E are forced Idle; relays A and B are unknown.
2. Relays A, B, and F are forced Active; relay C is forced Idle; relays D, E, and G are unknown.
3. Relays B and F are forced Active; relays D and E are forced Idle; relays A, C, and G are unknown.
4. Relay F is forced Active; no relay is forced Idle; relays A, B, C, D, E, and G are unknown.
5. Relays F and G are forced Active; no relay is forced Idle; relays A, B, C, D, and E are unknown.

P200-F03-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Six Boolean flags A, B, C, D, E, and X describe a permitted configuration. “P only if Q” means P implies Q; “P unless Q” means that if Q is false, P must be true. These are one-way requirements. Unspecified flags may be true or false if all requirements hold. A is true only if B is true and C is false. D is true unless A is true. D is true only if C is true. E is true only if D is false. X is true only if B is true. Exactly two of A, D, and E are true. Classify B, C, and X, in that order: T means true in every permitted configuration, F means false in every configuration, and U means both values occur in permitted configurations.

1. (T, F, F)
2. (U, F, U)
3. (T, F, U)
4. (T, U, T)
5. (F, T, U)

P200-F03-004
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A configuration assigns true or false to P, Q, R, S, T, and U. An “only if” statement gives a necessary condition, and “S unless P” means that P being false requires S to be true. No converse or closed-world assumption is supplied. The requirements are: P only if Q; Q only if R; R only if P; S unless P; S only if T is false; and U only if T is true. Exactly three of the five flags P, Q, R, S, and U are true. T is confirmed true but is not included in that count. Across every configuration satisfying all these requirements, what are the statuses of P, R, and U? Use T for always true, F for always false, and U for genuinely variable.

1. (T, T, U)
2. (U, U, F)
3. (F, F, T)
4. (T, U, F)
5. (T, T, F)

P200-F03-005

Six flags A, B, C, D, E, and F may each be true or false. “A unless B” means not-B implies A; “A only if E” means A implies E. Inclusive “or” permits both alternatives. Apply these meanings throughout. A holds unless B holds, and C holds unless D holds. Exactly one of B and D holds. A holds only if E holds. C holds only if E is false. E holds only if F holds, and F holds only if A or C holds. Finally, exactly two of A, C, and F hold. No other facts are supplied. P200-F03-006
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A permitted configuration assigns Boolean values to L, M, N, P, Q, and R. “Only if” introduces a necessary condition; “P unless Q” means that Q being false requires P to be true. A volunteer has arranged them at different heights so visitors can see them comfortably. Near the entrance, a small cabinet contains paper, spare pencils, tape, and a collection of postcards. The postcards were donated after an exhibition and are kept for future craft activities.

A notice describes a reading group that discusses short stories. Participants bring their own notebooks, share observations about the writing, and sometimes read a favourite passage aloud. The description emphasizes attentive listening and an open conversation about different interpretations. It also explains that visitors may simply listen during their first meeting. The reading group has no connection to the people, objects, or rules in the decision problem.

The rear corridor leads to a courtyard with benches and large planters. The plants include herbs and climbing vines. A caretaker stores a watering can nearby and checks the soil before watering. The courtyard is used for informal conversations when the weather is pleasant. A mural on the outer wall depicts an imaginary landscape with winding paths and a distant shoreline. Its shapes were chosen by the artists for visual balance.

Another display describes how a fabric banner was made. Several pieces were cut, arranged, stitched, and attached to a backing. The makers experimented with textures and kept small samples of the materials. The display includes photographs of the unfinished banner and a paragraph about the workshop atmosphere. These photographs and descriptions are background documentation, not additional clues about the decision problem.

A shelf beside the common room holds magazines, folded leaflets, and a guest book. Some visitors leave a few sentences about their experience. Other visitors draw a tiny picture or simply sign their name. The guest book belongs to this separate community-centre description. P200-F04-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A card contains six entries A, B, C, D, E, and F. Each entry is either true or false. The card need not be uniquely determined.

Use these conventions:
- NOT(P) reverses the truth value of the entire expression P.
- (P AND Q) is true exactly when both expressions are true.
- ONE(P,Q,R) is true exactly when one of its three arguments is true. An argument may itself be a compound expression.
- “IF P THEN Q” is false exactly when P is true and Q is false; otherwise it is true.
Parentheses specify the complete scope of each operator.

A card is allowed exactly when all three requirements hold:
- Exactly three of A, B, C, D, E, and F are true.
- NOT(ONE(NOT(A), B, C)) is true.
- Exactly one of the following three conditional statements is false: “IF A THEN D”, “IF B THEN E”, and “IF C THEN F”. The other two statements are true.

There are no further restrictions. Which listed expression is true for every allowed card?

1. ONE(A, (D AND NOT(E AND F)), (B AND E))
2. ONE(A, (D AND NOT(E AND F)), (B AND C))
3. ONE(A, (D AND NOT(E AND F)), (C AND F))
4. ONE(A, (D AND NOT(B AND F)), (B AND C))
5. ONE(A, (D AND NOT(C AND E)), (B AND C))

P200-F04-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A panel has four lamps, A, B, C and D. Each lamp is lit or unlit, and exactly two of the four lamps are lit. Four notes, N1 to N4, are attached to the panel. Each note carries exactly one label, TRUE or FALSE.

Reading rules:
- Square brackets fix scope exactly, so 'not [X]' denies the whole of X.
- 'or' is inclusive.
- 'if X then Y' is false only when X holds and Y fails; otherwise it is true.
- 'exactly one of (...)' and 'at least two of (...)' count how many of the semicolon-separated items inside the parentheses hold.
- 'Nk is true' means that note Nk carries the label TRUE.

N1: Not [exactly one of (A is lit; B is lit; C is lit)].
N2: At least two of (B is lit; D is lit; not [C is lit or N4 is true]).
N3: Not [if (N1 is true) then (C is lit)].
N4: Exactly one of (N1 is true; N2 is true; N3 is true; N4 is true).

A scenario is a choice of which two lamps are lit, together with a label for every note, such that every label is accurate. A note carries TRUE exactly when its statement holds. Each statement is evaluated using that same scenario's lamp states and labels, including a note's own label wherever it is mentioned. Two scenarios are different if they differ in at least one lamp state or at least one label.

How many different scenarios are there?

1. 3 scenarios
2. 6 scenarios
3. 5 scenarios
4. 8 scenarios
5. 4 scenarios

P200-F04-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Four Boolean flags P, Q, R, and S contain exactly two true flags. Define X to mean “exactly one of P, Q, and R is true.” Define Y to mean that all three expressions P or S, not Q, and R implies S are true. Every “or” is inclusive; an implication is false only when its antecedent is true and its consequent false. A further requirement says it is not the case that exactly one of X and Y is true. This requirement applies to the complete claims X and Y, not separately to their clauses. Consider every assignment satisfying both the two-flag count and this further requirement. Which statement must be true in every such assignment?

1. Y implies P.
2. Q implies P.
3. Q implies (P or R).
4. R implies S.
5. Not P implies Q.

P200-F04-004
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A grid has three named rows a, b, and c and two columns, left and right. Each of its six cells is independently either filled or empty unless constrained below. Consider three complete claims: C1 says every row contains at least one filled cell. C2 says some row contains two filled cells. C3 says exactly one of the two columns has a filled cell in every row. Exactly one of C1, C2, and C3 is true, and C1 is confirmed false. Count each complete claim once when applying the exactly-one requirement. The grid is otherwise unspecified, and multiple grids may be permitted. Which statement must hold for every permitted grid?

1. Exactly one row has two filled cells.
2. At least one row is full and at least one row is empty.
3. Exactly one row is empty.
4. There are exactly two filled cells altogether.
5. Each column has exactly one filled cell.

P200-F04-005
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A, B, C, and D are Boolean flags, with D confirmed true. Define X as “exactly two of A, B, and C are true.” Define Y as “it is not the case that B, C, and D are all true.” Define Z as “at least one of these two complete conjunctions is true: A and D; not B and C.” Thus the second conjunction requires B to be false and C true. Exactly one of X, Y, and Z is true. All flags other than D are otherwise unspecified, and all satisfying assignments count. Which implication is true in every satisfying assignment? An implication with a false antecedent counts as true; no implication below is a definition of its flags.

1. B implies C.
2. C implies A.
3. Not A implies not B.
4. Not B implies not D.
5. C implies B.

Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Four boxes a, b, c, and d may be red, striped, both, or neither. Exactly two boxes are red and exactly two are striped. Define three complete claims: C1: every red box is striped. C2: some striped box is not red. C3: it is not the case that exactly one box is both red and striped. Exactly one of C1, C2, and C3 is true. The negation in C3 applies to the entire exactly-one claim. No individual box's properties are given, and every property assignment meeting the requirements is permitted. Which pair gives the required number of boxes with both properties, followed by the number with exactly one of the properties? Count boxes, not true property labels.

1. (0, 4)
2. (1, 2)
3. (2, 0)

5. (2, 2)

P200-F05-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Let $U = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$ be a finite domain and let $\mathcal{F} = \{A, B, C, D\}$ be the family of four overlapping subsets of $U$ defined by
$$A = \{2, 3, 4, 6\}, \quad B = \{4, 5, 6, 7\}, \quad C = \{1, 3, 4, 5, 7\}, \quad D = \{1, 3, 7\}.$$
Two subsets $X \subseteq U$ and $Y \subseteq U$ satisfy all four of the following conditions:

1. **(Shared witness in $X \setminus Y$):** There exists an element $u \in X \setminus Y$ (that is, $u \in X$ and $u \notin Y$) such that for every set $S \in \mathcal{F}$, $u \in S$ if and only if $S \cap Y \neq \emptyset$.
2. **(Distinct witnesses in $X$):** For every set $S \in \mathcal{F}$, there exists a witness $w_S \in S \cap X$ such that the four witnesses $w_A, w_B, w_C, w_D$ are pairwise distinct, and for each $S \in \mathcal{F}$, $w_S \in Y$ if and only if every set $T \in \mathcal{F}$ containing $w_S$ satisfies $T \cap Y \neq \emptyset$.
3. **(Intersection threshold on $Y$):** For every element $y \in Y$, $y \in X$ if and only if every set $S \in \mathcal{F}$ containing $y$ satisfies $|S \cap Y| \ge 2$.
4. **(Non-containment in $X$):** For every set $S \in \mathcal{F}$, there exists an element $z \in S$ such that $z \notin X$.

Which subset of $U$ is the symmetric difference $X \triangle Y$, that is, the set of all elements in $U$ that belong to **exactly one** of $X$ and $Y$?

1. $\{1, 3, 4, 5\}$
2. $\{1, 4, 5, 7\}$
3. $\{1, 3, 4, 7\}$
4. $\{1, 2, 4, 5, 7\}$
5. $\{2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$

The complete universe is Ada, Ben, Cy, and Dana. The source group is {Ada, Ben, Cy}; eligible witnesses are {Ben, Cy, Dana}. The complete allowed-witness lists are Ada: Ben, Dana; Ben: Cy, Dana; Cy: Ben, Cy; Dana: Ada, Cy. Every pair not listed is forbidden. A witness must be eligible and different from its source, so a listed self-pair cannot be used. Consider three claims: I, every source has at least one witness; II, one single object can witness every source; III, it is possible to choose one witness for each source with all three chosen witnesses distinct. For III, sources choose simultaneously and no further restrictions apply. Which combination of truth values for I, II, and III is correct?

1. True, true, false
2. True, false, false
3. False, false, true
4. True, false, true
5. True, true, true

The universe is {a,b,c,d,e,f}. Red objects are {a,b,c}, blue objects are {b,c,d}, and green objects are {c,e,f}. Each red object must receive one witness that belongs to exactly one of blue and green. A witness must differ from its source, and the three chosen witnesses must be pairwise distinct. The complete allowed lists are a: {b,c}; b: {b,d}; c: {b,d,e,f}. Lists give permission only; property membership and the self-witness restriction still apply. Objects outside the red set need no witnesses and need not be used. Consider complete assignments satisfying all these requirements. What is the exact set of objects that can serve as c's witness in at least one such assignment?

P200-F05-004

The universe is {a,b,c,d}; a subgroup P is unknown and could initially be empty. Every member of P must be assigned one witness from {c,d}, different from itself. A universal requirement on members of P does not by itself assert that P is nonempty; the count and witness requirements must be considered together. P200-F05-005
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Two sources, a and b, each need a reviewer and a checker chosen from {c,d,e}. Allowed reviewers are a: {c,d}, b: {d,e}; allowed checkers for either source are {d,e}. Reviewers must be distinct from each other, and checkers must be distinct from each other. One object may occupy both roles for the same source only when that object is d. Across the four roles, exactly three different objects must be used. If a's checker is e, b's reviewer must be e. No other restrictions apply. Each option gives a's (reviewer, checker), then b's (reviewer, checker). Which listed assignment satisfies every requirement, including the restrictions that connect the two sources?

1. a:(d,d); b:(e,e)
2. a:(c,e); b:(d,d)
3. a:(d,e); b:(e,d)
4. a:(c,d); b:(e,d)
5. a:(c,d); b:(d,e)

P200-F05-006
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

The complete universe is {a,b,c,d}. A directed relation has exactly these outgoing lists: a:{b,c}; b:{a,c}; c:{a,b,d}; d:{c}. Every unlisted pair, including every self-pair, is absent. Sources are {a,b}, and targets are {c,d}. An intermediate witness must differ from its source. Compare these claims about two-edge routes: I, for every source and every target, there is an intermediate giving a route from that source to that target. II, for every source, one intermediate gives routes to both targets. III, one intermediate gives routes from both sources to both targets. Routes in all claims require both listed edges; witnesses may differ only where the quantifier order permits. Which exact set of claims is true?

1. {II}
2. {I}
3. {I,II}
4. {I,III}
5. {I,II,III}

Unrelated background material follows. It describes a different building and does not add or change any rule, event, relationship, observation, or record in the problem.

The community centre has a broad entrance with a woven mat and a display of drawings from a local workshop. The drawings show gardens, bicycles, clouds, and ordinary household objects. A volunteer has arranged them at different heights so visitors can see them comfortably. Near the entrance, a small cabinet contains paper, spare pencils, tape, and a collection of postcards. The postcards were donated after an exhibition and are kept for future craft activities.

A notice describes a reading group that discusses short stories. Participants bring their own notebooks, share observations about the writing, and sometimes read a favourite passage aloud. The description emphasizes attentive listening and an open conversation about different interpretations. It also explains that visitors may simply listen during their first meeting. The reading group has no connection to the people, objects, or rules in the decision problem.

The rear corridor leads to a courtyard with benches and large planters. The plants include herbs and climbing vines. A caretaker stores a watering can nearby and checks the soil before watering. The courtyard is used for informal conversations when the weather is pleasant. A mural on the outer wall depicts an imaginary landscape with winding paths and a distant shoreline. Its shapes were chosen by the artists for visual balance.

Another display describes how a fabric banner was made. Several pieces were cut, arranged, stitched, and attached to a backing. The makers experimented with textures and kept small samples of the materials. The display includes photographs of the unfinished banner and a paragraph about the workshop atmosphere. P200-F06-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Eight markers A, B, C, D, E, F, X and Z are compared using a reflexive, transitive relation ≤. Not every pair need be comparable. Write U=V for a tie, meaning both U≤V and V≤U; write U<V when only the first direction holds; and write U∥V when neither direction holds.

The protected facts are:
A<X<C, B<D, E<Z<F, and A∥F.
These facts cannot be discarded.

There are sixteen optional notes, arranged in two columns below. Each cell is one separate note, even when it follows from other notes. A tie note counts as one note, although it requires both directions.

row | column I | column II
a | C≤B | D≤E
b | C=B | D=E
c | D≤A | F≤B
d | D=A | F=B
e | A≤B | B≤E
f | B≤A | E≤B
g | C≤D | D≤F
h | D≤C | F≤D

For any chosen subset of notes, construct its result as follows. Start with the forward directions of the protected strict comparisons and all directions required by the chosen notes. Take the smallest reflexive, transitive relation containing those directions. Add no other comparisons. The subset is legal only if this resulting relation preserves every protected strict comparison and still has A∥F. Thus a subset that forces a reverse direction of a protected strict comparison is illegal.

Choose a legal subset retaining as many individual notes as possible. There is no further preference among maximizing subsets. Which option correctly gives the maximum number retained and describes the relation between X and Z across the maximizing results?

1. Maximum 6 notes; X∥Z in every maximizing result.
2. Maximum 7 notes; Z<X in every maximizing result.
3. Maximum 7 notes; some maximizing results have Z<X and others have X∥Z.
4. Maximum 7 notes; X∥Z in every maximizing result.
5. Maximum 8 notes; X∥Z in every maximizing result.

P200-F06-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Eight mineral samples—A, B, C, D, E, F, G, and H—each have an exact real-valued hardness rating. Two samples are tied (X = Y) if and only if they have the exact same rating; otherwise one is strictly harder than the other (X > Y or X < Y). A weak inequality X >= Y means that either X > Y or X = Y. The absence of a direct comparison between two samples does not imply equality.

Calibration of the eight-sample batch establishes two global structural constraints:
1. Tier limit: Across all eight samples, there are at most 4 distinct hardness ratings.
2. Tie limit: No three samples share the exact same hardness rating (at most 2 samples can be tied at any single rating).

Direct pairwise tests on the batch yield the following seven results:
- Strict inequalities: A > B and D > E
- Weak inequalities: B >= C, C >= D, F >= C, C >= G, and H >= D

Across all assignments of hardness ratings to the eight samples that satisfy all of the above constraints, which statement accurately describes the guaranteed and possible relationships for the pairs (G, E), (F, B), (F, H), and (B, H)?

1. G = E is guaranteed; F >= B is guaranteed (both F > B and F = B are possible); F != H is guaranteed (both F > H and F < H are possible); and all three of B > H, B = H, and B < H are possible.
2. G = E is guaranteed; F >= B is guaranteed (both F > B and F = B are possible); and all three relations (>, =, and <) are possible for both (F, H) and (B, H).
3. G = E is guaranteed; F > B is guaranteed (because F = A must hold); F > H is guaranteed; and only B > H and B = H are possible for (B, H).
4. D >= G >= E holds with both G > E and G = E possible; F >= B is guaranteed (both F > B and F = B are possible); F != H is guaranteed (both F > H and F < H are possible); and all three of B > H, B = H, and B < H are possible.
5. G = E is guaranteed; all three of F > B, F = B, and F < B are possible; F != H is guaranteed (both F > H and F < H are possible); and all three of B > H, B = H, and B < H are possible.

P200-F06-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Six objects A, B, C, D, E, and F have a reflexive, transitive comparison relation “at least as high as.” A tie means the relation holds both ways. Strictly higher means it holds forward but not backward. Incomparable means neither direction holds. These are properties of the relation, not merely missing notes. The supplied constraints are: A and B are tied; B is strictly higher than C; D is at least as high as A; E is at least as high as D; and C and F are incomparable. Any complete relation satisfying these rules is permitted; unmentioned pairs are not automatically incomparable or tied. Which combined conclusion must hold?

1. E is strictly higher than C, and E and F are incomparable.
2. D and A are tied, and F is strictly lower than E.
3. E is strictly higher than D, and F and A are incomparable.
4. E is strictly higher than C, and F is not at least as high as E.
5. E and A are tied, and F is strictly lower than D.

P200-F06-004
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

An object has an ordered pair of integer coordinates. It is at least as high as another object exactly when neither coordinate is smaller. It is strictly higher when it is at least as high and at least one coordinate is larger; equal pairs are tied; otherwise a pair with one coordinate larger and the other smaller is incomparable. Let A=(x,1), B=(1,y), and C=(0,2), where x and y each belong to {0,1,2}. Require A to be incomparable with C, and require B not to be strictly higher than A. The two requirements apply jointly. Which option lists exactly all permitted pairs (x,y), including possibilities involving a tie or incomparability between A and B?

1. {(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)}
2. {(1,0),(1,1),(1,2),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)}
3. {(1,0),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)}
4. {(0,0),(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1),(2,2)}
5. {(1,0),(1,1),(2,0),(2,1)}

P200-F06-005

Four objects have a reflexive, transitive “at least as high as” relation. A tie holds in both directions; a strict comparison holds in only one direction. Objects may also be incomparable. P200-F06-006
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A, B, C, and D have a reflexive, transitive comparison relation. “X strictly exceeds Y” means X is at least Y but Y is not at least X. A tie means both directions hold, and incomparable means neither holds. The constraints are: A strictly exceeds B; C is at least B; D strictly exceeds C; and A and D are incomparable. C may be tied with B or strictly exceed it, provided all other constraints still hold. Do not turn an unmentioned comparison into a tie or into a declared incomparability. 2. Incomparable only
3. Strictly higher or incomparable

Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Nine tasks must be scheduled on two stations, X and Y, within the time window from 0 to 24. Every task must run exactly once, without interruption, for its listed duration. Start times must be nonnegative integers, and every task must finish by time 24. Nothing has been started before time 0.

A task occupies every station listed for it throughout its run. Each station can serve at most one task at a time. Tasks using different stations may run together; there is no separate worker limit. A task requiring both stations must occupy them simultaneously for its entire duration.

All intervals are half-open: a task starting at s with duration d occupies [s, s+d). Thus, one task may start exactly when another finishes. Station X is unavailable during [4,6), and station Y is unavailable during [8,10). Neither a task nor any part of it may overlap a closure of a station it requires. Outside these closures, both stations are available throughout the planning window.

Every listed predecessor must finish no later than the task's start. A dash means there are no predecessors. Apart from these requirements, tasks may be ordered freely, and stations may be left idle.

Task | Duration | Required stations | Predecessors
A | 3 | X | —
B | 2 | Y | A
C | 3 | X | B
D | 4 | Y | —
E | 2 | X | D
F | 3 | Y | E
G | 3 | X | —
H | 2 | Y | G
I | 2 | X and Y | C, F

What is the smallest possible time by which all nine tasks can be finished?

1. Time 15
2. Time 16
3. Time 17
4. Time 18
5. Time 19

P200-F07-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Rules. Time is counted in whole minutes from minute 0, and every task must start at an integer minute. A task of duration d that starts at minute s occupies the half-open interval [s, s+d): it holds every station listed for it, all at once, from minute s up to but not including minute s+d. Tasks cannot be paused, split or moved to another station once started. A station of capacity c can hold at most c units at any minute; a task needing 2 units of a station takes 2 of its c. Two tasks that only touch (one ends at minute t, the other starts at minute t) do not overlap. "X -> Y" means Y cannot start before X has ended. A closure [a, b) means the station holds nothing during minutes t with a <= t < b; a task needing that station may end exactly at a or start exactly at b but may not overlap the closure. Closures are fixed clock times and do not move with the schedule. The makespan is the minute at which the last task ends. Unless stated otherwise, every task may start as early as minute 0.

A lab must process three samples. Stations: Bench (capacity 1); Analyzer A (capacity 1); Analyzer B (capacity 1); Review Desk (capacity 1).
Each analysis task (X1, X2, X3) runs on exactly one analyzer, chosen when it starts; its duration depends on the analyzer.
Tasks:
- P1 (prepare sample 1): 2 min, needs Bench.
- X1 (analyse sample 1): [A] 6 min, needs Analyzer A OR [B] 9 min, needs Analyzer B.
- R1 (review sample 1): 2 min, needs Review Desk.
- P2 (prepare sample 2): 2 min, needs Bench.
- X2 (analyse sample 2): [A] 3 min, needs Analyzer A OR [B] 6 min, needs Analyzer B.
- P3 (prepare sample 3): 1 min, needs Bench.
- X3 (analyse sample 3): [A] 6 min, needs Analyzer A OR [B] 7 min, needs Analyzer B.
- R3 (review sample 3): 5 min, needs Review Desk.
Precedence: P1 -> X1, X1 -> R1, P2 -> X2, P3 -> X3, X3 -> R3.

Question: (a) What is the minimum possible makespan? (b) List every assignment of analyzers to (X1, X2, X3) for which some schedule achieves that minimum makespan.

1. Minimum 14; only analyzer assignment (A,A,A).
2. Minimum 15; only analyzer assignment (B,A,A).
3. Minimum 14; only analyzer assignment (B,A,A).
4. Minimum 14; exactly the assignments (B,A,A) and (A,B,A).
5. Minimum 16; only analyzer assignment (A,A,A).

P200-F08-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Five vaults at an archive are numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 consecutively from west to east, so that Vault 1 is the westernmost vault and Vault v is immediately west of Vault v + 1 for each v in {1, 2, 3, 4}. In a valid assignment:
- Five archivists (Ada, Ben, Cy, Dia, and Eli) are assigned one-to-one to the five vaults.
- Five relics ( the Flute, the Globe, the Harp, the Mask, and the Ring) are assigned one-to-one to the five vaults.
- Five numbered keys (Key 1, Key 2, Key 3, Key 4, and Key 5) are assigned one-to-one to the five vaults.
- For each k in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}, Key k opens Vault k, and no vault holds the key that opens itself.

The assignment must also satisfy all five of the following conditions:
1. The key in the Flute's vault opens the Globe's vault, and the key in the Globe's vault opens the Flute's vault. Moreover, the Flute's vault number is smaller than the Globe's vault number, and their two vault numbers sum to 5.
2. Ada's vault holds the Harp. The key in Ada's vault opens the Mask's vault, and the key in the Mask's vault opens Ben's vault.
3. Eli's vault number is exactly 2 greater than the number of the key held in Vault 5.
4. If Eli's vault holds the Globe, then Ada is assigned to Vault 1.
5. The number of the key held in Cy's vault is strictly greater than the number of the key held in Dia's vault.

Which of the following statements is a forced fact that must hold in every valid assignment?

1. Dia's vault holds the Flute.
2. Ada is assigned to Vault 2.
3. Dia is assigned to the vault immediately west of Eli's vault.
4. Cy is assigned to Vault 4.
5. The key in Dia's vault opens Cy's vault.

P200-F09-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Six switches A, B, C, D, E and F each have two states: on and off. Initially A, C and E are on, while B, D and F are off. Each trial starts again from this initial state, turns off exactly one of A, C and E, turns on exactly one of B, D and F, and changes nothing else. Different pairs of choices count as distinct trials.

After each trial, evaluate reports R1–R8 below in order. Every reference to a report concerns its truth value in that same trial. Reports are statements to evaluate, not requirements that a trial must satisfy. “Same truth value” includes both being false. For a report with an “if … otherwise …” structure, its truth value is the truth value of the branch selected by its condition.

R1: A and D have the same state.

R2: Exactly one of B, C and F is on.

R3: If E is on, R2 is false; otherwise, R1 is true.

R4: R1 has the same truth value as the assertion “B is on and R2 is true.”

R5: Exactly two of R1, R2, R3 and R4 are true.

R6: If R3 is true, exactly one of R2 and R5 is true; otherwise, R1 and R4 have the same truth value.

R7: The assertion “Exactly three of R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 and R6 are true” has the same truth value as the assertion “B and F have the same state.”

R8: If R7 is true, exactly one of the assertions “R2 is true” and “B is on” is true; otherwise, R4 and R6 have the same truth value.

How many distinct trials result in exactly four of the eight reports being true?

1. 1 trial
2. 3 trials
3. 4 trials
4. 5 trials
5. 2 trials

P200-F09-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

An engineering audit evaluates six communication relays—R1, R2, R3, R4, R5, and R6—each assigned to one of three frequency Bands (K, X, or S, with two relays per Band) and recorded with an Output (in watts), a Buffer (in GB), and an Error count:

- R1: Band K, Output 40, Buffer 12, Errors 1
- R2: Band X, Output 55, Buffer 6, Errors 0
- R3: Band K, Output 60, Buffer 16, Errors 3
- R4: Band S, Output 35, Buffer 20, Errors 2
- R5: Band X, Output 50, Buffer 14, Errors 2
- R6: Band S, Output 45, Buffer 10, Errors 1

Each relay is evaluated under two operational classifications:
- A relay is Prime if and only if its Error count is strictly less than 3 and at least one of the following holds: (i) its Output is at least 50, or (ii) its Buffer is at least 12 and its Band is not S.
- A relay is Stable if and only if the other relay in the same Band is Prime and at least one of the following holds for the relay itself: (i) its Error count is 0, or (ii) its Output plus twice its Buffer is at least 70 (Output + 2 * Buffer >= 70).

The audit log contains four Primary Claims (P1–P4) and four Secondary Claims (S1–S4):

- P1: Exactly three relays are Prime, and every Stable relay has a strictly greater Output than every non-Stable relay.
- P2: At most one relay has a Prime status that differs from its Stable status (that is, is Prime but not Stable, or is Stable but not Prime).
- P3: In every Band, either both relays have the same Stable status, or the relay in that Band with the larger Buffer is Prime.
- P4: If P1 and P2 have different truth values, then the sum of the Error counts of all Stable relays is strictly greater than the sum of the Error counts of all non-Stable relays.

- S1: Either P3 is true, or every relay that is both Prime and Stable has an Output plus Buffer strictly greater than 60 (Output + Buffer > 60).
- S2: Exactly two of the Primary Claims (P1–P4) are true if and only if at least one relay that is neither Prime nor Stable has an Error count strictly less than 2.
- S3: If S1 is true and P2 is false, then among the relays with a Buffer of at least 12 GB, strictly more are Stable than are Prime.
- S4: If P4 and S3 are not both true, then the number of Prime relays with an Error count of 0 or 2 equals the number of true claims among P1, P2, and S1.

Exactly how many Primary Claims (P1–P4) and how many Secondary Claims (S1–S4) are true?

1. 2 Primary Claims and 2 Secondary Claims (4 true claims in total)
2. 2 Primary Claims and 3 Secondary Claims (5 true claims in total)
3. 3 Primary Claims and 2 Secondary Claims (5 true claims in total)
4. 3 Primary Claims and 3 Secondary Claims (6 true claims in total)
5. 1 Primary Claim and 3 Secondary Claims (4 true claims in total)

P200-F09-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

The complete universe is {1,2,3,4,5,6}. Red objects are {1,2,5}; tall objects are {2,3,5,6}. Evaluate six descriptive reports in numbered order, using the supplied sets and the truth values of earlier reports. Printed reports are not premises requiring their own truth. R1: exactly two red objects are tall. R2: every red object is tall. R3: R1 is false or R2 is true. R4: exactly one of R1 and R2 is true. R5: the number of true reports among R1, R3, R4 equals the number of red objects that are not tall. R6: R3 and R5 have the same truth value. “Or” is inclusive, and each complete report counts once. How many of all six reports are true?

1. Two
2. Four
3. Three
4. Five
5. One

A multiset contains the six entries 1,1,2,3,3,4. Repetitions count as separate entries, but a distinct value is counted only once. Evaluate these descriptive reports using the data and earlier report truth values. R1: exactly three distinct values occur once. R2: there are four distinct values. R3: the sum of the entries exceeds twice the number of entries. R4: R1 is false and R2 is true. R5: exactly two of R2,R3,R4 are true. R6: neither R4 nor R5 is true. R7: if R5 is true, R1 is true. 2. (2,3)
3. (3,1)
4. (1,2)

Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A token is either white or black, not both. There are no other restrictions on the speakers' types or the token's color.

Here, “or” includes the possibility that both claims hold. “If and only if” is true exactly when its two sides have the same truth value.

Each speaker makes exactly this statement:

A: “The token is white, and exactly one of B and C is a truth-teller.”
B: “D and E are of the same type: both truth-tellers or both liars.”
C: “A is a liar or F is a truth-teller.”
D: “Exactly two of A, C, and F are truth-tellers.”
E: “The token is white if and only if B is a liar.”
F: “D is a liar and E is a truth-teller.”

A consistent assignment specifies every speaker's type and the token's color so that all six statements obey the truth-teller/liar rule simultaneously. For each consistent assignment, record the pair (token color, total number of truth-tellers among the six speakers).

Which option gives exactly the set of attainable pairs? Every pair it lists must occur, and no unlisted pair may occur. Different consistent assignments may yield the same pair.

1. Exactly {(black, 2), (white, 4)}.
2. Exactly {(white, 2)}.
3. Exactly {(white, 2), (white, 3), (white, 4)}.
4. Exactly {(white, 2), (white, 4)}.
5. Exactly {(black, 4), (white, 2), (white, 4)}.

D: ((exactly 1 of [E, (not H), Y]) xor G)
E: (G iff (H xor Y))
F: ((exactly 1 of [B, D, Y]) xor (not C))
G: ((exactly 1 of [(not H), F, (not X)]) xor (not A))
H: ((exactly 2 of [A, (not F), X]) iff (not B))
Consider ALL consistent assignments. First minimize the TOTAL number of truthful speakers. Restrict attention to assignments attaining that global minimum. Which option gives both this minimum and exactly all attainable (X,Y) pairs among those minimizing assignments? 1 means on and 0 means off.

1. Minimum 3; pairs {(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)}.
2. Minimum 3; pairs {(0, 0), (1, 0), (1, 1)}.
3. Minimum 3; pairs {(0, 1), (1, 0), (1, 1)}.
4. Minimum 4; pairs {(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)}.
5. Minimum 2; pairs {(0, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)}.

B: ((A and (not D)) implies (F xor (not L)))
F: ((exactly 1 of [D, (not G), K]) xor C)

C: (B iff (F xor (not L)))
D: ((exactly 2 of [C, B, (not L)]) iff (not F))

The actual assignment is unknown, and both values of H are consistent. You may ask A exactly ONE additional yes/no question from the options. P200-F11-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A communications array consists of five relays—A, B, C, D, and E. In a valid configuration, each relay X is assigned an integer tier t(X) in {1, 2, 3} and a role r(X) in {Primary, Backup} subject to five base specifications:

1. Global Allocation: The sum of the tiers of all five relays is 10, and each of the three tiers (1, 2, and 3) is assigned to at least one relay. Exactly three relays are assigned the Primary role and two are assigned the Backup role.
2. Role-Tier Coupling: Every Tier-3 relay is Primary, and every Tier-1 relay is Backup. (Tier-2 relays may be either Primary or Backup.)
3. Priority and Backup Uniqueness: Relay A has a strictly higher tier than Relay B (t(A) > t(B)). Furthermore, no Backup relay other than B itself may share the same tier as B (for every Backup relay X != B, t(X) != t(B)).
4. Conditional Symmetry: If Relay E is a Tier-2 Backup relay, then Relay C has a strictly higher tier than Relay D (t(C) > t(D)); otherwise, Relays C and D have the same tier (t(C) = t(D)).
5. Routing Triggers: If Relay A is assigned Tier 3, then Relay D is Primary; if Relay A is assigned Tier 2, then Relay E is Backup.

An engineer evaluates the target conclusion
Q: "Relay C is assigned the Primary role."
under three independent supplementary hypotheses, each tested separately by appending it alone to the five base specifications:
- Hypothesis I: The sum of the tiers of the three Primary relays is an even number.
- Hypothesis II: Relay A has a strictly higher tier than Relay C (t(A) > t(C)).
- Hypothesis III: Relay A's tier exceeds Relay B's tier by exactly 1 (t(A) - t(B) = 1).

For each hypothesis, classify the status of conclusion Q across all valid configurations satisfying the base specifications plus that hypothesis, using the following four categories:
- Entailed: At least one configuration satisfies the combined rules, and Q holds in every such configuration.
- Refuted: At least one configuration satisfies the combined rules, and Q is false in every such configuration.
- Contingent: At least one configuration satisfying the combined rules makes Q true, and at least one makes Q false.
- Inconsistent: No configuration satisfies the combined rules.

Which option correctly classifies (Hypothesis I, Hypothesis II, Hypothesis III)?

1. Hypothesis I: Refuted; Hypothesis II: Contingent; Hypothesis III: Entailed
2. Hypothesis I: Inconsistent; Hypothesis II: Refuted; Hypothesis III: Entailed
3. Hypothesis I: Inconsistent; Hypothesis II: Entailed; Hypothesis III: Contingent
4. Hypothesis I: Inconsistent; Hypothesis II: Contingent; Hypothesis III: Entailed
5. Hypothesis I: Refuted; Hypothesis II: Refuted; Hypothesis III: Contingent

P200-F12-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Five boxes labeled A, B, C, D, E occupy positions 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, respectively. Initially, they contain tokens numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, respectively, one token per box.

Exchanging whole boxes moves the boxes together with their tokens; labels stay attached to boxes. Exchanging tokens leaves the boxes in place. A token “at a position” is the token in the box currently there. “Left of” means at a strictly lower-numbered position. Every instruction and condition uses the current state, not the initial state.

Three routines are performed, each exactly once, in an unknown order. Each routine finishes before another begins, and its instructions run from top to bottom.

Routine X:
• Exchange the whole boxes at positions 1 and 4.
• If the token in box A is smaller than the token in box C, exchange the tokens at positions 2 and 5. Otherwise, exchange whole boxes B and D.

Routine Y:
• Exchange the tokens in boxes A and D.
• If the box containing token 1 is left of box B, exchange the whole boxes at positions 2 and 3. Otherwise, exchange the tokens in boxes C and E.

Routine Z:
• Exchange whole boxes C and E.
• Exchange the tokens at positions 1 and 3.
• If the token at position 4 is odd (1, 3, or 5), exchange whole boxes A and B. Otherwise, do nothing.

After all three routines, the token at position 2 is observed to be even (2 or 4). No other observation is available.

What is the complete set of possible ordered pairs (token number in box B, token number at position 1) consistent with this observation? Each option is a set: the order in which its pairs are listed does not matter.

1. {(1, 5), (5, 1)}
2. {(1, 5), (2, 1)}
3. {(3, 2), (5, 1)}
4. {(1, 1), (5, 5)}
5. {(1, 5), (3, 2)}

P200-F12-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Five fixed slots, numbered 1 through 5 from left to right, each hold one of five movable boxes labeled A, B, C, D, and E. Each box contains one of five movable balls numbered 1 through 5. At any time, a box's slot number is the number of the slot it currently occupies, and its ball number is the number of the ball it currently contains. A box is aligned if its current slot number equals its current ball number.

Initially, before Step 1:
- Slot 1 holds Box A containing Ball 3.
- Slot 2 holds Box B containing Ball 5.
- Slot 3 holds Box C containing Ball 1.
- Slot 4 holds Box D containing Ball 2.
- Slot 5 holds Box E containing Ball 4.

Two swap operations can be applied to a pair of boxes (X, Y):
- Box-Swap: Boxes X and Y exchange their slots, carrying their current balls with them (the ball inside each box does not change).
- Ball-Swap: Boxes X and Y remain in their current slots, and only the balls currently inside them are exchanged.

A four-step automated sequence is executed. At the start of each step, an ordered pair of target boxes (First Target X, Second Target Y) is identified from the current state:
- Step 1: X is Box B; Y is the box currently containing Ball 4.
- Step 2: X is Box E; Y is the box currently in Slot 1.
- Step 3: X is the box currently in the slot whose number equals the ball number of Box A; Y is the box currently containing Ball 4.
- Step 4: X is Box C; Y is the box currently in the slot whose number equals the ball number of Box D.

Default Rule: At each step, if the current slot number of X is strictly less than the current ball number of Y, perform a Box-Swap between X and Y; otherwise, perform a Ball-Swap between X and Y.

An operator may either run all four steps under the Default Rule (no override) or apply a single override at exactly one step (Step 1, Step 2, Step 3, or Step 4). At the overridden step, the operator performs the opposite operation (Ball-Swap instead of Box-Swap, or Box-Swap instead of Ball-Swap) between the same two target boxes X and Y, while all other steps follow the Default Rule.

The operator wants to maximize the number of aligned boxes after Step 4 completes. Which policy achieves this maximum, and what is the resulting configuration after Step 4?

1. Override Step 1; after Step 4, Slot 1 holds Box A, Slot 2 holds Box B, and Box C contains Ball 3.
2. Override Step 2; after Step 4, Slot 1 holds Box A, Slot 2 holds Box E, and Box C contains Ball 1.
3. Override Step 3; after Step 4, Slot 1 holds Box E, Slot 2 holds Box A, and Box C contains Ball 3.
4. Override Step 4; after Step 4, Slot 1 holds Box C, Slot 2 holds Box A, and Box C contains Ball 3.
5. Use no override; after Step 4, Slot 1 holds Box A, Slot 2 holds Box C, and Box C contains Ball 1.

P200-F12-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Four fixed slots, numbered 1 through 4 from left to right, initially hold boxes A, B, C and D. Their contents are respectively red, blue, green and yellow tokens. A box keeps its name when moved. Exchanging contents leaves the boxes in place; exchanging boxes moves their contents with them. Perform these operations in order: exchange the contents of boxes A and C; exchange the boxes in slots 1 and 4; inspect the current token positions, and if blue is left of red, exchange the contents of slots 2 and 3, otherwise exchange the boxes in slots 2 and 4; finally exchange box A with the box currently containing yellow. Which token sequence is now in slots 1 through 4?

1. Yellow, red, blue, green
2. Green, blue, red, yellow
3. Green, red, blue, yellow
4. Red, green, blue, yellow
5. Yellow, blue, red, green

Fixed containers A, B, C and D initially contain tokens p, q, r and s respectively. Routine R exchanges A with B, then B with C. Routine S exchanges B with D, then A with C. Four fixed drawers, numbered 1 through 4 from left to right, initially contain the distinct tokens w, x, y and z in an unknown order. A machine first exchanges the contents of drawers 1 and 3. P200-F13-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Four boxes a, b, c, d each hold a number from {1, 2, 3, 4}. A switch t holds either 0 or 1. Initially,
(a, b, c, d, t) = (1, 3, 2, 4, 0).

Run exactly four rounds of the procedure below. The boxes and switch carry their values from one round to the next.

At the beginning of each round, save B = b, C = c, and D = d. These capital-letter values remain fixed throughout that round and are replaced by fresh copies at the beginning of the next round.

An assignment x ← y copies y's value into x without changing y. In a simultaneous assignment, every right-hand value is read before any of that assignment's changes occur. In an ordered sequence, each assignment finishes before the next begins. Anything not assigned retains its value. Unless a capital letter is shown, a test or assignment uses the current value at that point.

Perform these three steps in order during every round:

1. If t = 0, simultaneously assign a ← c and b ← a. Otherwise, simultaneously assign c ← b and d ← c.

2. Test whether a < d, using the values after step 1.
• If yes, perform this ordered sequence: b ← d; then d ← a; then a ← b.
• If no, perform this ordered sequence: d ← b; then b ← c; then c ← d.

3. Test whether the current b equals the saved C.
• If yes, simultaneously assign a ← B, c ← a, and t ← 1 − t.
• If no, simultaneously assign a ← D and d ← c, leaving t unchanged.

Each test is made once when its step is reached; changing a tested value does not restart any step. After step 3 of the fourth round, which listed tuple gives (a, b, c, d, t)?

1. (2, 4, 4, 2, 0)
2. (2, 4, 2, 2, 1)
3. (4, 2, 2, 4, 1)
4. (2, 2, 4, 2, 0)
5. (2, 4, 4, 2, 1)

P200-F13-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Start with x=3, y=7 and z=2. Save p=x and q=y; these saved values never change. Follow the steps below in order. Whenever a step says simultaneous, every right-hand side uses the values immediately before that step. First set x=y−z and y=x+z simultaneously. If the resulting x equals y, set z=p+z; otherwise set z=q−2z. Next save the current x as t, then simultaneously set x=y+z and y=q−t. If the resulting y is strictly less than p, increase z by y; otherwise decrease z by x. Finally, if z is strictly less than q, restore x to p; otherwise set y=p. What is the final ordered triple (x,y,z)?

1. (3,2,7)
2. (10,3,7)
3. (10,2,7)
4. (10,3,5)
5. (8,3,5)

P200-F13-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A circular list has four numbered positions and initially contains [2,5,1,4]. The cursor starts at position 2 and an accumulator starts at zero. Perform exactly three rounds. At the beginning of each round, save the value under the cursor as v. If v is odd, exchange that entry with the next clockwise entry; if v is even, exchange it with the previous entry. Next add the saved v to the accumulator, and overwrite the entry currently under the cursor with the new accumulator. Finally move the cursor two positions clockwise. Positions wrap between 4 and 1, and all parity tests and additions use the saved v, not a replacement value. Which final list and cursor position result?

1. [2,5,10,15]; position 1
2. [2,14,4,9]; position 4
3. [5,14,2,9]; position 2
4. [2,14,5,9]; position 4
5. [2,9,5,14]; position 2

P200-F13-004

Three original cards form the list [3,1,4]. Start a running total at zero and visit those three original cards once, in their original left-to-right order. P200-F13-006

Seven tasks ($A, B, C, D, E, F, G$) each execute continuously over a single closed time interval $[s_X, e_X]$ with integer endpoints satisfying $0 \le s_X < e_X \le 12$. The duration of task $X$ is $d_X = e_X - s_X$. Every task has a duration of at least $2$, and all seven durations $d_A, d_B, d_C, d_D, d_E, d_F, d_G$ are pairwise distinct.

Interval relations between tasks are defined by their exact endpoints:
- $X$ meets $Y$ ($X \to Y$) if $e_X = s_Y$.
- $X$ starts-with $Y$ ($X \vdash Y$) if $s_X = s_Y$ and $e_X < e_Y$.
- $X$ ends-with $Y$ ($X \dashv Y$) if $s_Y < s_X$ and $e_X = e_Y$.
- $X$ strictly contains $Y$ ($X \supset Y$) if $s_X < s_Y$ and $e_Y < e_X$.

At any integer time $t \in \{0, 1, \dots, 12\}$:
- Task $X$ covers $t$ (closed-endpoint semantics) if $s_X \le t \le e_X$. Let $C(t)$ be the number of tasks that cover $t$.
- Task $X$ spans $t$ (open-interior semantics) if $s_X < t < e_X$. Let $S(t)$ be the number of tasks that span $t$.

The seven tasks satisfy the following relational and instantaneous constraints:
1. $B \vdash A$ and $B \to C$.
2. $E \dashv C$ and $E \to D$.
3. $D \dashv F$ and $F \supset A$.
4. $G \supset E$.
5. $(C(3), S(3)) = (5, 2)$.
6. $C(4) = S(4)$.
7. $(C(8), S(8)) = (6, 3)$.
8. $(C(10), S(10)) = (4, 2)$.

Which of the following gives the exact intervals of tasks $A$, $E$, and $F$, along with the pair $(C(5), S(5))$?

1. $A = [0, 10]$, $E = [6, 8]$, $F = [0, 12]$, and $(C(5), S(5)) = (4, 4)$
2. $A = [1, 10]$, $E = [4, 8]$, $F = [0, 11]$, and $(C(5), S(5)) = (5, 5)$
3. $A = [1, 10]$, $E = [5, 8]$, $F = [0, 11]$, and $(C(5), S(5)) = (5, 4)$
4. $A = [1, 11]$, $E = [5, 8]$, $F = [0, 12]$, and $(C(5), S(5)) = (5, 5)$
5. $A = [1, 10]$, $E = [5, 8]$, $F = [0, 12]$, and $(C(5), S(5)) = (5, 4)$

P200-F14-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Three sessions occupy half-open intervals: a session ending at time t is inactive at t, so touching endpoints do not count as overlap. Session A runs from 1 to 6. B lasts four units and starts at one of 3, 4 or 5. C lasts three units and starts at one of 4, 5, 6 or 7. The overlap of A and B lasts at least two units. C cannot start before A ends, and B and C overlap for at least two units. No other constraints apply and there are no other sessions. For every arrangement satisfying these conditions, how much time in total has exactly one session active? Count separated portions together.

1. 2 units
2. 3 units
3. 4 units
4. 5 units
5. 6 units

P200-F14-003
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Bookings occupy half-open intervals within the window [0,14); touching bookings do not overlap. A is fixed at [1,5). B lasts four units and may start at 5, 6 or 7. C lasts three units and may start at 8, 9, 10 or 11. B and C must overlap for exactly one unit, and neither may overlap A. A maintenance job needs a single uninterrupted interval during which no booking is active; it may start at 0 or exactly when a booking ends and must finish by 14. You may choose any permitted starts for B and C. What is the greatest maintenance duration that can actually be scheduled?

1. 1 unit
2. 2 units
3. 4 units
4. 5 units
5. 3 units

P200-F14-004
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A is active on [0,6). B lasts five units and starts at an integer b in {2,3,4}. C ends at 10 and starts at an integer c in {4,5,6,7}. Every interval includes its start and excludes its end; an instantaneous touch is not overlap. The overlap duration of A and B is exactly three units. The overlap duration of B and C is either two or three units, with both possibilities permitted if the other conditions allow them. No start or end is otherwise fixed. Which statement must hold in every permitted arrangement? When a statement gives a total duration, combine all separate portions satisfying it.

1. Exactly two intervals are active for a total of four units.
2. At least two intervals are active for a total of five units.
3. All three intervals overlap for a positive duration.
4. C starts strictly after A ends.
5. B and C overlap for exactly three units.

P200-F14-005
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Exactly three activities take place inside the observation window [0,20). Their durations are five, six and six units. Each activity occupies one uninterrupted half-open interval entirely inside the window. Endpoints may coincide, but touching has zero overlap duration. The sum of the three pairwise overlap durations is eight units: time shared by all three contributes separately to each of those three pairwise overlaps. The duration shared by all three is exactly one unit. These measurements are consistent, but the individual start times have not been supplied. What are the total durations with exactly one activity active and with no activity active, respectively? Separated portions contribute to the same total.

1. 1 unit; 11 units
2. 4 units; 9 units
3. 7 units; 10 units
4. 4 units; 10 units
5. 5 units; 12 units

P200-F14-006
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A occupies [0,6). B starts at an integer b in {2,3,4,5} and lasts four units. C starts at an integer c in {4,5,6,7,8} and lasts three units. All intervals include their start and exclude their end. An overlap must have positive duration; intervals may touch without overlapping. B must overlap A. C must not overlap A, but it must overlap B for at least two units. P200-F15-001
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Two robots, A and B, stand on a movable platform over a fixed coordinate grid. East increases x; north increases y. The point O=(0,0) is fixed in the outside world, not marked on the platform. There are no edge effects. A robot at (x,y) has distance score |x|+|y| to O.

A platform turn rotates both robots' positions and headings around the stated pivot, including the pivot robot's heading. The pivot robot's position stays fixed during that turn. A robot's own right turn is 90° clockwise; its left turn is 90° counterclockwise. Walking never changes a heading. All actions below occur in the stated order, and references to a heading use its value at that moment.

Initially, A is at (0,0), facing east, and B is at (2,1), facing north.

A hidden selector names either A or B. Both of the first two platform turns use the selected robot's current position as pivot. Each turn is 90°, but its direction is hidden: either clockwise or counterclockwise, with no assumed relation between the two directions.

Perform these actions:
• Make the first hidden platform turn.
• A turns right, then walks two units forward.
• B moves one unit in the direction currently to A's right, without changing B's heading. B then turns left.
• Make the second hidden platform turn.

At this checkpoint, A faces north, and B's distance score to O is strictly smaller than A's. These are the only observations supplied.

Continue from the checkpoint:
• A walks two units backward.
• B turns right, then walks one unit forward.
• The platform turns 90° clockwise about B's current position, regardless of the hidden selector.
• A moves one unit in the direction currently to its own left, without turning.

Which option gives exactly the set of possible final positions of A, over all hidden choices consistent with the checkpoint observations?

1. {(0,-1), (0,1)}
2. {(4,-1), (4,1)}
3. {(4,-3), (4,-1)}
4. {(3,-2), (3,0)}
5. {(3,0), (3,2)}

P200-F15-002
Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

A navigation test takes place on a 2D integer grid. In the **Global Frame**, coordinates are $(x, y)$ where $+x$ is East, $-x$ is West, $+y$ is North, and $-y$ is South, with cardinal headings $\{\text{N}, \text{E}, \text{S}, \text{W}\}$.

At any moment, a **Rover** has a global position $(x, y)$ and a heading $H \in \{\text{N}, \text{E}, \text{S}, \text{W}\}$ that defines its **Local Frame**:
- The local **Forward** axis ($+f$) points in the direction of $H$ (with **Backward** as $-f$).
- The local **Right** axis ($+r$) points $90^\circ$ clockwise from $H$ (with **Left** as $-r$).
A local displacement or relative coordinate pair $(f, r)$ means $f$ grid units along the Rover's current Forward axis and $r$ grid units along its current Right axis.

**Initial State (Step 0):**
- The **Rover** is at global position $(0, 0)$ facing **North** ($\text{N}$).
- A mobile **Beacon** is at global position $(4, 5)$.

**Mission Rules (Steps 1 to 4):**
The test runs for 4 sequential steps (Step 1, Step 2, Step 3, Step 4). During **each** step:
1. The **Beacon** translates in the **Global Frame** by $1$ unit West and $1$ unit South, i.e., $(\Delta x, \Delta y) = (-1, -1)$.
2. Simultaneously, the **Rover** executes one of four command modules—**A**, **B**, **C**, **D**—using each module **exactly once** across the 4 steps:
   - **Turn-then-Move**: The Rover first updates its heading $H$, and then translates in the local frame defined by its **new** heading.
   - **Move-then-Turn**: The Rover first translates in the local frame defined by its **current** heading (before turning), and then updates its heading $H$.

**Command Modules:**
- **Module A (Turn-then-Move):** First turn $90^\circ$ Right (clockwise) relative to current heading; then move $2$ units Forward and $1$ unit Left in the local frame, $(f, r) = (2, -1)$.
- **Module B (Move-then-Turn):** First move $3$ units Forward and $1$ unit Right in the local frame, $(f, r) = (3, 1)$; then turn $90^\circ$ Left (counterclockwise) relative to current heading.
- **Module C (Turn-then-Move):** First turn $180^\circ$ (reverse) relative to current heading; then move $2$ units Forward and $2$ units Right in the local frame, $(f, r) = (2, 2)$.
- **Module D (Move-then-Turn):** First move $1$ unit Backward and $2$ units Left in the local frame, $(f, r) = (-1, -2)$; then align heading to **Global West** ($\text{W}$), regardless of prior heading.

**Telemetry Logs** (recorded at the end of each specified step, after both the Beacon and the Rover have completed that step's full maneuver):
- **Log 1 (End of Step 2):** In the Rover's local frame, the Beacon lies **directly Backward** of the Rover ($f < 0$ and $r = 0$).
- **Log 2 (End of Step 3):** In the Rover's local frame, the Beacon lies strictly in the **Front-Left quadrant** ($f > 0$ and $r < 0$).
- **Log 3 (End of Step 4):** The Rover's local Forward–Backward axis is parallel to the **Global North–South axis** (its final heading is either Global North or Global South).

At the end of Step 4, what is the Rover's global position $(x, y)$, and what are the Beacon's coordinates $(f, r)$ in the Rover's local frame?

1. Rover at global $(6, 0)$; Beacon at local $(1, -6)$
2. Rover at global $(1, 5)$; Beacon at local $(-4, -1)$
3. Rover at global $(-2, 2)$; Beacon at local $(1, -2)$
4. Rover at global $(0, 6)$; Beacon at local $(-5, 0)$
5. Rover at global $(2, 2)$; Beacon at local $(-1, -2)$

Use only the information in this problem. Apply its stated rules exactly. Choose exactly one of the five numbered options. Choose a final answer, not an explanation. Do not assume an unstated fact.

Six people each wear one badge. The table gives their starting badges and two directed relations. A person's guide and reviewer are always the people listed in that person's row; these relations never change and need not be reciprocal.

Person | Guide | Reviewer | Starting badge
Anya | Davi | Esme | amber
Bram | Finn | Cora | blue
Cora | Anya | Finn | coral
Davi | Esme | Bram | green
Esme | Bram | Anya | ivory
Finn | Cora | Davi | violet

Before anything moves, assign three labels:
• Caller is the reviewer of the guide of the person wearing coral.
• Witness is the guide of the reviewer of the person wearing amber.
• Visitor is the person whose reviewer is Witness.

These labels name people and keep referring to those same people throughout, regardless of badge movements.

Now exchange three badges simultaneously: Caller gives their badge to Witness, Witness gives their badge to Visitor, and Visitor gives their badge to Caller. Everyone else keeps their badge. No badges move again.

Give a single marker to Witness. Perform exactly three passes of the marker, using this same rule each time:
• Find the current marker-holder's guide.
• Look up the badge that this guide wore at the start, before the exchange.
• Find the person wearing that badge now.
• Give the marker to that person's reviewer.

All lookups for a pass are completed before its marker transfer. The next pass starts with the new marker-holder. In particular, a starting badge is looked up in the table, while its current wearer is determined after the exchange.

Who holds the marker after the third pass?

1. Esme
2. Bram
3. Davi
4. Cora
5. Finn
